questions.q: In the lab, 0.1% of the weights are made 30 times larger. What does that do to int8 with one scale for the whole matrix, and to int8 with a scale per 32 weights?
options: Both stay near 0.01, because int8 has enough levels
Both error figures rise by the same factor of about 14
One scale: error 0.0106 to 0.1476. Scale per 32: 0.0053 to 0.0094
One scale improves, because the largest weight sets a finer grid
questions.answer: One scale: error 0.0106 to 0.1476. Scale per 32: 0.0053 to 0.0094
questions.why: The largest weight sets the step for every weight that shares its scale, so one outlier coarsens the whole matrix. A block confines it to 32 weights. See the table in the Lab section.

questions.q: Why does FP8 E4M3 with one scale keep the same error, 0.0265, with and without the planted outliers?
options: FP8 stores a separate scale for every weight
Its spacing grows with the value, so small weights keep their relative precision
It clips the outliers away before rounding
E4M3 has more mantissa bits than int8
questions.answer: Its spacing grows with the value, so small weights keep their relative precision
questions.why: A float's gap between neighbours scales with the number itself (CU-210). The scale puts the largest weight at 448, so nothing is clipped, and the price is precision: E4M3 has only 3 mantissa bits.

questions.q: How many bits per weight does GGUF Q4_0 use, and where does the half bit above 4 come from?
options: 4.0, because the scale is kept in a separate file
4.25, from an 8-bit scale per 32 weights
5.0, because each weight carries its own scale
4.5, from one fp16 scale shared by each block of 32 four-bit codes
questions.answer: 4.5, from one fp16 scale shared by each block of 32 four-bit codes
questions.why: block_q4_0 in ggml-common.h is one ggml_half (16 bits) plus 16 bytes of nibbles for 32 weights: (32 · 4 + 16) / 32 = 4.5.

questions.q: Going from int8 to int4 at a scale per 32 weights multiplied the clean-data error by 18.2 in the lab. What predicts that figure?
options: The ratio of the bit counts, 8 / 4
The ratio of the grid steps, 127 / 7 = 18.1
The square root of 12
The block size, 32
questions.answer: The ratio of the grid steps, 127 / 7 = 18.1
questions.why: The step is max|w| / qmax and the RMS rounding error is step / √12, so for the same weights the error scales as 1 / qmax.

questions.q: A card has no native kernel for a quantized format in a checkpoint. What does ComfyUI do with those layers?
options: It refuses to load the checkpoint
It keeps the weights quantized and dequantizes them to the compute dtype for the matrix multiply
It rewrites the checkpoint as fp32 on disk
It switches the layers to GGUF
questions.answer: It keeps the weights quantized and dequantizes them to the compute dtype for the matrix multiply
questions.why: get_disabled_quant_formats lists the formats the device cannot compute natively, pick_operations logs them as emulated ops, and QUANTIZATION.md describes dequantizing for compute-dtype execution when the fast path is disabled.

questions.q: What does this lab tell you about which format gives the best pictures?
options: That GGUF Q4_0 does, because it has the lowest 4-bit error
That FP8 always beats int8
That a scale per row is enough for every model
Nothing: it measures weight and matmul error on synthetic Gaussian weights, not images
questions.answer: Nothing: it measures weight and matmul error on synthetic Gaussian weights, not images
questions.why: The What is contested section says the same: real weight distributions differ, the outliers were planted by us, and the effect on pictures and speed is an empirical question per model and card.
